title: The Name remains
hookLine: naam rahio saadhoo rahio: the Name remains, the holy remain, the Guru remains (Salok M9 56, ang 1429)

lines: A WEEK OF THINGS TAKEN AWAY.
cards: For a week now these saloks have been taking things away. Rama and Ravana, gone. Youth, gone.
Strength, gone. Friends, gone. Whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow.
Then comes salok fifty-six, and the whole list turns over. After all that subtraction, he finally names what doesn't go: three things, said in one breath, each with the same verb.
And then a sting in the tail about how few people notice them.

teach.b: Salok fifty-six, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind. Rahio means remained, stayed, abides.
The Name remains. The saadhoo, the holy one, the true devotee, remains. The Guru, God, remains.
Three things, one verb, like three posts driven into ground that everything else is washing over. The Name, naam, stands at the center of Sikh devotion: God's presence, remembered and repeated.
The saadhoo is the person who lives in that remembrance. Gurbani speaks often of the saadh sangat, the company of such people, and of how their example outlasts them.

teach.h: THE NAME, THE HOLY, THE GURU.
teach.b: And gur gobind here isn't the tenth Guru's name: in this line it's God as Guru, the teacher who is also the Lord.

teach.h: GUR GOBIND HERE: GOD AS GURU.
teach.b: The second line is the sting.

teach.h: HOW RARE THE ONE WHO REPEATS IT.
teach.b: In paraphrase: Nanak says, in this world, how rare is the one who has repeated the Guru's mantra. So the three things that last are there for anyone, and the salok says few pick them up.
That's the shape of the whole collection. All week the world was a dream, a show, a wall of sand. That wasn't gloom for its own sake.
It was clearing the table so you could see what was still on it. Everything on the table passes.
The Name, the people who live it, and God are still there when the table is cleared.

how: Salok fifty-six is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers present it as the answer to the saloks about passing.

o: a call to the holy to come and stay awhile
a cry of grief for what has been lost
remains, abides, still there when all goes

games.q: the Name remains — tap the pairs.
p: the holy one who lives the Name

s: gur gobind in this salok names Guru Gobind Singh
in this line it's God as Guru, the teacher who is also the Lord.
salok fifty-six names three things that remain
the Name, the holy, and the Guru: three things, one verb.
the salok says everyone picks up the Name
its second line says how rare it is.

games.q: after a week of saloks taking things away, what does salok fifty-six do?
o: names what remains: the Name, the holy, the Guru.
games.why: the list turns over. all the passing was clearing the table so you could see what was still on it.

practice: Think back over what these saloks took away, youth, strength, friends who drifted, and then ask a different question: what has stayed?
Maybe a faith, a person who's always been there, a practice, a line like this one; name one thing quietly to yourself. If you pray, repeat Waheguru slowly, as one way of picking up what remains.

wordCard.voice: Rahio, remains, stays, abides. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind: the Name, the holy, and God as Guru all rahio when everything else goes.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saadhoo, the holy one, a devotee who lives in the Name; one of the three things that remain.

carryVoice: Your line: still there when it's cleared. The table empties, and three things stay. Day six hundred seven, done.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 56 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)
